---
title: "Study 03 — Large vacuum droplets"
subtitle: "(H₂O)₂₀ / ₃₀ / ₅₀ · GFN2 vacuum · 3 ps"
---

## Size suppresses evaporation

Scaling the free clusters up, every size holds together as a single droplet at
low bias: stable radius of gyration, zero molecules evaporated, all O–H intact —
the **opposite** of the tiny n=2–4 clusters, and with GFN2 retained (no periodic
box needed).

| n | R_g start → end | fraction in droplet | evaporated | O–H |
|---|-----------------|:-------------------:|:----------:|:---:|
| 20 | 3.61 → 3.96 Å | 1.00 | 0 | intact |
| 30 | 4.45 → 4.18 Å | 1.00 | 0 | intact |
| 50 | 4.99 → 4.95 Å | 1.00 | 0 | intact |

![Radius of gyration stays flat and no molecule evaporates, all three sizes
(low bias).](assets/droplet_stability.png){width=680}

## …and reveals a bias-scaling artifact

Raising `kpush` from 0.008 → 0.05 at n = 30 barely perturbs the droplet. That is
**not** intrinsic robustness: the bias is a function of **global** RMSD spread
over all degrees of freedom, so the same nominal `kpush` is far gentler on a
90-atom droplet than on a dimer.

::: {.callout-important}
## Implication
A single `kpush` number does not transfer across system sizes. This is the
empirical case for a **size-normalized** (per-molecule / per-atom) bias.
:::
